title: After an extraordinary wave, what comes next?
subtitle: The “smart” conventional wisdom is: midterms don’t predict future elections. I’m not sure about that for a profoundly unpopular lame duck.
contentHtml:
We’d like to extend another word of thanks for following FLIPR, our midterm election coverage, and our liveblog last night. We’re really pleased with how everything went, and I can’t express how much more fulfilling it is to run our own business than to work for a big, careless corporation.

I do need to catch up on rest after we published seven stories, plus the liveblog, within a three-day window. That’s not typical for us; we aim for something more like three newsletters per week, plus regularly updating a host of models and statistical tools. Nor are those all politics posts; we also regularly cover sports, AI and sometimes some “wild card” topics. (To control what types of emails appear in your inbox, see here.)

I’m also aware that one can go overboard on post-election recriminations: I think we probably did that in 2024, for instance. On our agenda for the year ahead: rebuilding RAPTOR (our NBA model) and possibly extending PELE, our soccer model, to European club football; beginning our coverage of the 2028 presidential election (sorry, not sorry), probably including some polling tools; expanding our coverage of AI; and a site redesign. We also may be doing some hiring.

Still, last night’s results deserve deeper consideration than most elections.

As measured by the change in the House popular vote, they featured the second-biggest midterm swing since World War II, which should be around 15 points toward Democrats once all votes are counted.

The biggest midterm waves since World War II

Democrats will gain 7 to 9 Senate seats — Alaska and Mississippi are pending — along with flipping around 45 House seats and, once all votes are counted in Kansas, probably 6 governorships. Unlike some recent Democratic maps that were concentrated in smaller coastal states, these occurred broadly in basically every corner of the country. (Well, except Florida, as usual.) Once new terms begin, Democrats will control the governorships in states totaling around three-quarters of the U.S. population; in the Electoral College, this would translate to a 392-146 landslide.1

There were plenty of signature wins too. Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932. Not only did James Talarico win by double digits in Texas; Gina Hinojosa flipped the governorship there. Keisha Lance Bottoms became the nation’s first Black female governor. They won a Senate seat in South Carolina, and if prediction markets are right, they’ll flip Mississippi too. The repudiation that Democrats have been waiting 10 years for against Donald Trump finally came, and bigly.

Friend-of-the-newsletter Sean Trende has written that this was a “100-year flood”, the usual nomenclature of waves and tsunamis not quite sufficing. There are deep implications for the future of the Democratic Party, the Republican Party and the Supreme Court, and we’ll be covering all of that. Polls (and models) also had a lot on the line, although the results take some care to interpret. On the one hand, the results back up our theory that the direction of polling bias is unpredictable; on the other hand, it was a pretty big and broad lowballing of Democrats.

But let’s keep today’s post relatively simple. I’ll look at what happened after other waves of roughly this magnitude. This is the seventh time since World War II that a midterm featured a swing of 10 points or more; the others were 1946, 1966, 1974, 1994, 2006 and 2010. For each one, I’ll ask a few simple questions: what caused the wave, how similar it is to this year, and most importantly, what came next.

As I expressed to Ezra Klein before the election, this midterm felt “momentous” because it potentially reflects the end of the Trump Era and the transition into … well, who knows what. But two years ago, everyone was talking about a conservative “vibe shift”, and that obviously didn’t pan out.

1946 (13.2-point swing)

When it happened: During Harry Truman’s first (unelected) term.

Outcome: Republicans gained 55 House seats, 12 Senate seats and 3 governorships.

Why it happened:

  • An abrupt shift from the wartime to the peacetime economy, which had produced a recession in 1945, followed by supply-chain shortages, high inflation and strikes;

  • Truman’s lower stature as compared to FDR and his low popularity ratings;

  • Perhaps pent-up backlash toward Democrats and lots of viable targets after four consecutive FDR terms.

What happened next: Truman upset Thomas Dewey in 1948, and Democrats made unusually large gains in Congress for a presidential year, basically fully reversing their 1946 losses. However, Truman was unpopular for much of his second term. Not officially a lame duck — the 22nd Amendment exempted him — he stood down after considering a third term in 1952, and Dwight D. Eisenhower won in a landslide.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? Politically speaking? I’d argue no. The end of World War II was a huge inflection point for the world, of course, and marked the emergence of the United States as a hegemonic superpower. But when I’ve covered this in the past, I consider everything from 1932 through 1968 to be part of “The Long Liberal Era”, with FDR and LBJ ushering in the New Deal and Great Society, respectively. Eisenhower was a notably moderate Republican, meanwhile, in an era of high bipartisan comity.

Applicability to 2026: If you follow politics, you’ll have a direct memory of some elections. The first one I remember watching — really just fragments, flickers of Reagan’s dominant map on the network newscasts — was in 1984. But the elections your parents remember will also be part of the “training set”: the collective memory that shapes conventional wisdom about how elections work. 1946 came before either of those, and that probably biases me against wanting to think it’s particularly relevant to today. You can draw some parallels: is the emergence of AI like the end of the war? And pent-up fatigue: Trump hasn’t had three terms in a row, but it feels like he has. Overall, this seems like a stretch.

1966 (12-point swing)

Outcome: Republicans gained 47 House seats and 3 Senate seats, although they failed to take control of either chamber; they also added 8 governorships, mostly west of the Mississippi.

When it happened: During LBJ’s second — but first elected — term. Like Truman, he therefore wasn’t a true lame duck, but dropped out of the 1968 race after a close call in the New Hampshire primary that was treated as a vote of no confidence.

  • Increasing opposition to the Vietnam War on the left;

  • Increasing opposition to the Civil Rights movement and the hippies on the right;

  • Republicans were starting from a very, very low floor during a period in which they routinely got trounced in elections to Congress;

  • LBJ had brought sweeping changes to the welfare state.

What happened next? 1968 was competitive, with Hubert H. Humphrey nearly winning the popular vote, but Nixon was re-elected in a landslide in 1972. Overall, Republicans won the presidency in 5 of 6 elections, excepting only 1976.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? Yes, I’d say: I think it was the precursor to the transition from the Long Liberal Era to the Long Conservative Era.

Applicability to 2026: Well, there’s a parallel in the form of a stupid war that nobody was asking for. And although LBJ wasn’t constitutionally a lame duck, he was on his back heel. But in other ways, the comparison is weaker. LBJ really did have an enormous mandate after his landslide in 1964, something that Trump never did.

1974 (11.2-point swing)

Outcome: Democrats gained 45 House seats, developing an enormous majority, along with 4 Senate seats and 4 governorships.

When it happened: Amid Gerald Ford’s lone (unelected) term after Nixon resigned the presidency in August 1974 following Watergate.

Why it happened: Watergate and inflation.

What happened next? A dark-horse Democratic nominee, Jimmy Carter, only narrowly beat Ford before losing in a landslide to Ronald Reagan in 1980 in an election that also produced massive gains in Congress for Republicans.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? No. Carter was not exactly transformational, and his presidency looks like a blip in the Long Conservative Era.

Applicability to 2026: People love this one, citing corruption and the high cost of living as parallels. And although Ford wasn’t a lame duck, Nixon had been and, like Trump, had been a central political figure for a long time, having been elected vice president in 1952. But I’d argue it’s only a medium-good comp. 1974 had a relatively singular cause, and scandals don’t bother the American public in the way they once did; corruption might have been only third on the list of voter concerns about Trump after high gas prices and Iran.

1994 (12.1-point swing)

Outcome: Republicans picked up 54 House seats, 8 Senate seats, and 10 governorships.

When it happened: In Bill Clinton’s first term, after he’d won in 1992 with a strong Electoral College performance but not a majority of the popular vote.

  • The Clintons’ overreach on Hillarycare;

  • Bill Clinton’s personal scandals;

  • Although Clinton’s agenda wasn’t radical, we were in the midst of the Long Conservative Era;

  • Clinton had a tenuous mandate. Although he became popular following 1994, his first-term numbers more closely resembled the 43 percent of the vote he was elected with against George H.W. Bush and Ross Perot;

  • This was one of several elections (also 1972, 2010, 2016) that marked a series of step changes against Democrats in the rural South.

What happened next? Clinton performed a hard pivot to the center and was re-elected easily, although again without a popular-vote majority. His vice president, Al Gore, won the popular vote but lost the Electoral College to George W. Bush despite Clinton’s popularity and a strong economy.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? For me, no. Clinton was a centrist and triangulating president, which is why I see his presidency as being part of the Long Conservative Era.

Applicability to 2026: It’s a stretch. Clinton was in his first term, and although you can argue he overread his mandate, this ranks higher than most waves on structural explanations. The Democrats’ “Solid South” was falling apart and partisanship began a sharp rise under Newt Gingrich.

2006 (10.6 points)

Outcome: Democrats netted 31 House seats, flipped 6 Republican-held Senate seats (winning both chambers) and gained 6 governor’s mansions.

When it happened: In George Bush’s second, lame-duck term, following a close re-election in 2004.

  • Bush’s ever-declining popularity amid fatigue with the War on Terror, his mishandling of Hurricane Katrina and his failed attempt at Social Security reform.

  • Bush governing as if he had a huge mandate when 2004 had been close.

  • Republican corruption and scandals.

  • Arguably, early warning signs of the mortgage bubble.

What happened next? Bush’s popularity continued to plummet; instead, the Republican nominee was John McCain, a Bush critic. But McCain nevertheless lost to Barack Obama by 7+ points, and Democrats had another huge year in Congress to rack up massive majorities in both chambers of Congress.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? Clearly yes; I consider 2006 to be basically the end of the Long Conservative Era and the start of the New Liberal Era under Obama and later Biden.

Applicability to 2026: Obviously quite high. You had basically the same ingredients: unpopular wars, unforced errors, and looming economic anxiety. It’s also the only true lame duck midterm on the list. I’ve argued before that there are sharp parallels between 2004 and 2024, including the media being convinced that America was a “center-right country” despite the narrowness of the Bush and Trump wins. And take a look at this comparison between Bush and Trump’s second-term approval ratings:

Trump and Bush second-term approval ratings have followed a nearly identical trajectory

2010 (17.4 points)

Outcome: Republicans hit the jackpot, picking up 6 Senate seats, 6 governorships, and 63 House seats.

When it happened: During Barack Obama’s first term, following his landslide win in 2008.

  • The weak economic recovery following the global financial crisis and persistently high unemployment;

  • Democrats had a broad list of targets to defend after consecutive landslides in 2006 and 2008, with particular exposure in rural districts where the demographics were turning against them;

  • They had charged ahead to pass Obamacare even after losing a special Senate election in Massachusetts;

  • Populist backlash was brewing amid the rise of the Tea Party, which now reads like a precursor to Trumpism;

  • Obama’s penchant for turning out younger, low-propensity voters, particularly minorities, worked out well in presidential years but poorly in midterms.

What happened next? Obama, in a well-executed campaign, rebounded to soundly defeat Mitt Romney, picking up 2 Senate seats in the process to bolster the Democratic majority but failing to flip the House. A turnout/enthusiasm gap was again a problem for him in 2014 amidst a tepid economy, but he left office as a relatively popular president by modern standards. But then Democrats nominated Hillary Clinton, and then came Trump.

Did it mark the end of an era/beginning of a new one? Not really. In some ways, it was kind of the reverse; this election was more of a market correction amid an emerging liberal era. Democrats would go on to win the popular vote for the U.S. presidency three more times in a row, with Obama’s vice president, Joe Biden, winning the Electoral College as a 77-year-old in 2020. But 2006/2008 only partly reflected a vibe shift involving changing cultural values on issues like gay marriage; there were also a lot of contingencies related to Bush, which didn’t have as much resonance once he was out of office, kept a low profile and tried his hand at painting.

Applicability to 2026: Strong in the sense that it’s the only swing of the same magnitude. But overall, relatively weak. Obama was in his first term, and had a far bigger mandate than Trump. Ironically, the parties have now swapped positions, and it was Trump who relied on low-propensity voters in his two Electoral College wins in 2016 and 2024 but has performed poorly in other elections.

So what can we learn from this?

Well, that’s not so straightforward.

Some experts have claimed that the predictive power of midterms is basically zero when forecasting forthcoming elections. (In fact, I’m guilty as charged; we published one such analysis at FiveThirtyEight.)

And it’s true that if you build a scatterplot of the magnitude of the midterm wave on the x-axis, and subsequent election results on the y-axis, it looks more or less random.

I have three critiques of this, though. One is a minor quibble: most midterms are waves, but analyses of elections like 2026 ought to focus on the ones that are similar in magnitude to it. With that said, there’s not much obvious signal: 2010 didn’t end up being all that bad for Barack Obama and Democrats, and even the public backlash to Watergate in 1974 didn’t persist for very long.

The second is that people tend to focus solely on the results of the next election two years later when long-term shifts are probably more important.

The main critique, however, is that these past midterm waves are very unlike one another. There are some common ingredients in play — overreaching one’s mandate, high exposure due to past success, dumb wars, etc. But the ratios are slightly different from election to election. In some cases, structural changes are a strong factor, and in others they don’t matter at all. In some years, like this one and in 1946, the president is extremely unpopular; in others, he’s only somewhat unpopular and the issue is more that there’s a relative decline from an election that brought large coattails.

The one crystal-clear parallel — I’d argue more than 1974 — is 2006, the only true lame-duck election on the list. That produced another landslide against Republicans two years later.

Am I just cherry-picking here? Yeah, kind of. Unfortunately, we sometimes have to do that in election analysis since we don’t get very many data points. I suppose my prior is that if we had 60 past elections instead of six, you would see some signal. But the point is, I think you’re allowed to be a little more qualitative when you don’t have enough reliable data points to fit a model anyway.

And one factor to consider is: how in the hell are Republicans going to go about picking an appealing candidate for 2028? JD Vance is the leader in prediction markets, but he’s Trump’s vice president. Marco Rubio, the other frontrunner, is the Secretary of State. I’m not sure there’s any John McCain looming on the horizon because it’s hard to be a McCain in Trump’s version of the Republican Party, which constantly excommunicates dissenters.

So really my argument is this. It seems unlikely to me that Trump’s approval rating, currently 38 percent, is liable to get all that much better. The decline in his numbers over the past two years has been remarkably persistent, instead. Plus, he’s 80 years old, and doesn’t seem to care about the implications of his unpopularity for anyone else in the Republican Party. I don’t think anyone is expecting him to attempt a Clintonian pivot, much less to pull it off. And the Republican nominee in 2028 will have to navigate an incredibly treacherous tightrope: distancing themselves just enough from Trump without triggering his ire. This produced a massive fail for Ron DeSantis last time around.

Until last night, you could at least argue that Trump’s low popularity was a mirage, a reflection of polls that weren’t capturing his real supporters. But not only did Republicans lose Senate seats in Texas (!) and South Carolina (!!) and Kansas (!!!) and maybe Mississippi (!!!!): Democrats were considerably underestimated by the polls. One theory for the polling miss, ironically, is that Trump is so unpopular that respondents won’t admit they once supported him, which can inflate Republican results in surveys that weight to past vote recall.

So, we’ll see. Democrats have plenty of their own problems, and last night didn’t erase them. We’re in an era when most presidential elections are close. I just don’t think you can witness last night without recognizing that Republicans are in a hell of a predicament. I’ll have more to say about this soon.
